Via Email March 31, 2026 The Honorable B rad Little Governor of Idaho 700 West Jefferson Street B oise, ID 83720 D ear Governor Little: We respectfully urge you to veto House B ill 542. We share the goal of protecting children online, but this bill will not accomplish that. The bill has loopholes that will allow online platforms popular with teens to avoid implementing safeguards, which fundamentally undermines the bill’s goal. The only platforms that are covered are those operated by companies earning $1 billion or more in annual advertising revenue, and that “primarily facilitate the uploading and sharing of content.” This means the bill fails to cover platforms that are widely used by Idaho teens because they fall outside an arbitrary revenue threshold. Other platforms may argue they are outside the scope of the law because they “primarily” facilitate messaging, not sharing content. A ll online platforms should be held to the same standard. Under this bill, they are not. This bill will likely lead to the collection of new and additional data about Idahoans to meet its requirements that each online platform continuously estimates the age of all users to a high level of confidence. For teens, platforms must obtain verifiable parental consent. This will involve parents sharing their ID s, children’s information, and other sensitive data. This process must be repeated for every app a teen uses, increasing the privacy and security risks. C ompanies will be forced to preserve that data indefinitely for compliance purposes and in anticipation of litigation due to the bill’s private right of action. Given the global scale of the mobile internet, some data will inevitably be sent to app developers located outside the United States. Parents consistently report that they prefer a single, secure place to approve app downloads—such as the app store—rather than navigating dozens of different approval and age verification methods across individual apps. Unfortunately, this bill does not offer that. Instead, it is a one-size-fits-all government mandate. It restricts online experiences for every teen under 17 years old, regardless of the parent’s preferences. A s one Senator described it during floor 1

discussion: “Parents cannot waive the requirements. If parents allow their children to be on social media, make an informed choice, the state is saying your judgment doesn’t count.” Under HB 542, platforms are expected to implement these new age estimation, parental consent, and content restriction systems within three months. That aggressive and unreasonable deadline was never intended to allow for compliance by companies operating in Idaho. Instead, it was intended to force the issue into litigation as quickly as possible. We respectfully request that you draw a firm line against legislative efforts designed to push the business community into litigation rather than compliance. D uring its final vote in the Senate, a bipartisan group of fourteen Senators voted no on HB 542. The vote tally represents a clear recognition among legislators regarding the problems with HB 542. These concerns include the undermining of parental authority, data and security risks as a result of sharing sensitive data with every app a teen uses, and the likelihood of a successful legal challenge. It also – critically – fails to address all the places where Idaho teens spend time online. We respectfully request that you veto HB 542. A veto of HB 542 is not a rejection of the goal to do more to protect teens’ online safety. Instead, it is a signal to the legislature to pursue a clear, workable, constitutional approach, rather than a bill likely to be tied up in court that ultimately helps no one. We believe that the best approach to online safety is to empower parents to make informed choices about their teen’s online experiences. Meta has made significant investments to create safe, age-appropriate experiences for teens across our platforms, like Teen A ccounts, giving parents peace of mind and more control over their teens’ online experiences. With Teen A ccounts, teens are automatically placed into protective settings that limit who can contact them and restrict the content they see. Teen A ccounts provide tools for parents to help supervise teens’ use of the platform. We stand ready to work with you to help empower parents and protect teens online. Respectfully, D an Sachs VP, State and Local Policy 2
